blocks.text: The MCP specification itself changes over time.
New capabilities get added, old ones occasionally get refined.
Protocol versioning is what lets an older client and a newer server, or the reverse, still talk to each other safely instead of breaking the moment one side updates before the other.
1. Where the Version Lives

blocks.alt: The initialize request carries the protocol version

blocks.text: The protocol version is announced by the client in its initialize request, and confirmed by the server in its initialize response.
This exchange happens once, right at the start of a session, before any other request is considered valid.

blocks.title: A quick self-check
blocks.content: If you can point to exactly which message carries the protocol version, you understand where this negotiation actually happens.

blocks.text: Nothing about this negotiation requires a separate handshake step, it rides along with the initialize exchange that already had to happen anyway.
2. Version Numbers Are Dates, Not Semantic Versions

blocks.alt: A date-based version is compared against a semantic version

blocks.text: MCP identifies protocol versions by release date rather than a traditional major dot minor dot patch scheme.
This makes it immediately obvious how old or new a given version actually is just by reading the string.
A date like 2025 dash 06 dash 18 immediately tells a reader roughly how recent that revision is, without needing to consult a separate release history.
It also avoids the ambiguity that sometimes comes with major and minor number schemes, where it is not always obvious how significant a change actually was.
3. What Happens When Versions Differ

blocks.alt: A client version is compared against a server version

blocks.text: If a client and server support different versions, the server typically responds with whichever version it supports that is closest to what the client asked for.
The client then decides whether it can still work correctly under that version, or whether it needs to fail gracefully instead.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Client wants","Server supports","Result"],"rows":[["2025-06-18","2024-11-05, 2025-06-18","Agree on 2025-06-18"],["2026-01-01","2024-11-05, 2025-06-18","Server falls back to its newest supported version"]]}

blocks.text: This fallback behavior is exactly why very few real sessions ever fail outright due to a version mismatch alone.
4. Backward Compatibility Within a Version Family

blocks.alt: An older client still works with a newer server

blocks.text: Most changes between versions are additive, a new optional capability, a new optional field.
An older client simply never asks for the new thing, and keeps working exactly as it did before, this additive discipline is what keeps the ecosystem stable as the spec evolves.

code.content:
# an older client simply never sends this newer optional field
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize", "params": {"protocolVersion": "2024-11-05"}}

blocks.text: This is precisely the discipline that keeps the wider MCP ecosystem from fragmenting into incompatible islands.
5. Breaking Changes Are Rare and Deliberate
Occasionally a change cannot be purely additive, an existing field needs new required behavior.
These changes are made deliberately and sparingly, since every breaking change forces every implementation still on the old version to update before they can talk to anything on the new one.
A breaking change is usually reserved for cases where continuing to support the old behavior would itself become a source of confusion or risk.

blocks.title: A useful framing
blocks.content: A breaking change is a last resort, chosen only when an additive alternative genuinely does not exist.

blocks.text: 6. Capability Negotiation Complements Versioning

blocks.alt: A protocol version pairs with capability negotiation

blocks.text: Version negotiation settles which overall protocol revision is in use.

Capability negotiation, covered in its own lesson in the MCP Architecture module, then settles which specific optional features within that version are actually available, the two work together, not as substitutes for each other.
Think of the protocol version as the language being spoken, and capabilities as the specific vocabulary within that language each side actually knows.
7. How a Client Should Handle an Unsupported Version

blocks.alt: An unsupported version leads to a graceful error

blocks.text: If a server responds with a version the client genuinely cannot work with at all, the client should fail clearly and early, rather than attempting to proceed and hitting confusing errors later.

code.content:
if server_version not in SUPPORTED_VERSIONS:
    raise RuntimeError(f"Unsupported protocol version: {server_version}")

blocks.title: A safer default
blocks.content: Failing loudly and immediately on a truly unsupported version beats limping along and producing confusing errors many steps later.

blocks.text: A clear error message naming the unsupported version also makes the fix obvious to whoever investigates it.
8. Pinning a Specific Version Deliberately
Some clients deliberately pin to a specific known-good protocol version, rather than always requesting the newest one.
This trades away access to brand new capabilities in exchange for predictable, well tested behavior.
A production system that has been thoroughly tested against one specific version might reasonably choose stability over always chasing the newest release.

blocks.title: A tradeoff to weigh
blocks.content: Staying pinned indefinitely eventually means missing genuinely useful new capabilities, most teams revisit their pinned version periodically rather than never.

blocks.text: 9. Reading Version Changes in the Specification
Each new protocol version typically comes with a changelog describing exactly what was added or changed.
Reading this before upgrading a client or server implementation is the fastest way to know whether any existing code needs adjustment.
Skipping this step and simply upgrading blindly is a common source of avoidable integration bugs.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Change type","Action needed"],"rows":[["New optional capability","None required, adopt when ready"],["Changed required field","Update before upgrading"]]}

blocks.text: 10. Testing Against Multiple Versions
A server intended for wide use often gets tested against more than one protocol version its likely callers might still be running.
This catches compatibility gaps before real users do.
Catching a regression here, before shipping, is far cheaper than discovering it from a support ticket later.
11. Version Negotiation Failure Is Not Common in Practice
Because MCP versions change infrequently and favor additive updates, an actual negotiation failure is rare.
Most real world friction comes from a specific capability being missing, not from the base protocol version itself being incompatible.
Most integration problems trace back to a missing capability check, not to the underlying protocol version itself.
12. Deprecation Instead of Sudden Removal

blocks.alt: An old feature gets a deprecation warning before later removal

blocks.text: When something genuinely does need to change in a breaking way, it is usually deprecated first.
A deprecated feature keeps working for a transition period, giving implementations time to migrate before it is removed entirely.
A deprecation notice usually comes with a recommended replacement, giving implementers a clear migration path rather than just a warning.
13. Version Awareness in Long Lived Deployments
A server that runs unmodified for a long time may end up talking to clients spanning several protocol versions at once.
Designing for that reality upfront, rather than assuming every caller is always on the latest version, avoids surprises later.
Monitoring which versions connected clients are actually using, similar to observability practices covered in the Production MCP module, makes this reality visible rather than assumed.
14. A Worked Example
Trace an older client connecting to a newer server, and the server gracefully falling back to a version both sides understand.

code.content:
client_version = "2024-11-05"
server_supported = ["2024-11-05", "2025-06-18"]
agreed_version = client_version if client_version in server_supported else server_supported[-1]

blocks.text: If the client had instead requested a version the server does not recognize at all, the same fallback logic still produces a usable, shared version both sides understand.
15. Common Mistakes When Handling Protocol Versions

items: Hardcoding a single expected version and breaking the moment either side updates.
Assuming every version difference means total incompatibility, most changes are additive and harmless.
Never testing against an older version a real client might still be running.
Confusing protocol versioning with capability negotiation, they solve related but distinct problems.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is treating a fallback to an older shared version as a failure, when it is actually the negotiation working exactly as intended.
16. Practice: Simulate a Version Mismatch
Write a small function that takes a client requested version and a list of server supported versions, and returns the version both sides should actually use.
Extend your function to also print a clear warning whenever the negotiated version differs from what the client originally requested.
This same logic, in a more complete form, is exactly what a real MCP client library performs automatically during every session initialize handshake.
Key Takeaway
Protocol versioning lets MCP keep evolving, adding new capabilities over time, without breaking clients and servers still running an older version.

This lesson closes the Communication Protocol module. The next module, Transport Mechanisms, moves from the message format itself to the actual pipes, stdio, HTTP, and more, those messages travel through.
The deprecation pattern from the newly added section is worth remembering, it is what gives real implementations time to adapt, rather than being broken overnight by a single protocol update.
